summary: Oswald Richter specialized in Iranian, Central Asian, and Indological studies. He completed his Ph.D. at the University of Leipzig under Karl Brugmann (~1892–1897), later serving as an ethnographic assistant at Dresden's Museum of Ethnology (1898) and at Berlin's Ethnological Museum (1904).

Otakar Klíma was an Iranian and Central Asian studies scholar and linguist. He earned his Ph.D. at Charles University (1927–1932) studying under Bedřich Hrozný, Vincenc Lesný, and Jan Rypka, later directing the Near Eastern Section at the Czech Academy of Sciences (1953–1973).

Otakar Pertold worked in Indology and religious studies, earning his Ph.D. (~1903–1908) and habilitation (~1908–1912) at Charles University under teachers including Josef Zubatý, Wilhelm Geiger, and Paul Deussen. He held several posts at Charles University from 1919 to 1955, becoming ordinary professor in 1934.

Indologist Othmar Frank studied at the University of Paris (~1814–1816), including Sanskrit under Alexander Hamilton. He served as professor of philosophy at the University of Bamberg (~1801–1803), professor at the University of Würzburg (1821), and professor at the University of Munich (1826).
Indologist Otoya Tanaka studied under Naoshiro Tsuji at the University of Tokyo (~1927–1930). He later held a professorship at Chuo University from ~1957 to 1974.

Otto Albert Paul specialized in linguistics and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied under Wilhelm Geiger and completed his Ph.D. (1924–1927) and habilitation (by 1938) at the University of Munich, later serving as director of the Institut zur Erforschung der Judenfrage (1941).

Archaeologist Otto Benndorf studied at the University of Bonn (~1857–1862) under Friedrich Wilhelm Ritschl and Friedrich Gottlieb Welcker, and at Göttingen. He held posts at Göttingen, Zurich, Munich, Charles University, and the University of Vienna, and served at the Austrian Archaeological Institute (1898–1907).
Otto Blau studied at Martin Luther University of Halle-Wittenberg (1848) and the University of Leipzig (~1848–1852), studying under August Friedrich Pott.

Linguist and Indologist Otto Donner earned his degrees at the University of Helsinki (M.A. ~1853–1861; Ph.D. ~1861–1863) and studied under Albrecht Weber, Heymann Steinthal, and Rudolf von Roth. He served as Professor of Sanskrit and Comparative Philology at Helsinki (1875–1905).

Otto E. Neugebauer was a historian of mathematics and science who studied under Boris Turayev and earned his Ph.D. at Göttingen (~1924–1926). He held posts at Göttingen, Copenhagen (1933–1939), Brown University (1939–1969), and the Institute for Advanced Study (1945, 1950, 1969–1990).

Otto Fischer worked in Sinology, Japanology, and art history, completing his habilitation at the University of Göttingen (~1910–1912). He served as director of the Staatsgalerie Stuttgart (1920), head of the Kunstmuseum Basel (1927), and associate professor at the University of Basel (~1927–1937).

Otto Franke specialized in Sinology and Indology, completing his Ph.D. at Göttingen under Franz Kielhorn (1884–1886) and studying under Carl Arendt and Wilhelm Grube. He held chairs at the Hamburgisches Kolonialinstitut (1909–1923), Hamburg (1910), and Berlin (1923–1931).

Otto Fredrik Tullberg was an Indologist and linguist who studied at Uppsala University (M.A. 1822–1830) and under scholars including Franz Bopp, Eugène Burnouf, and Horace Hayman Wilson. He became Professor of Oriental Languages at Uppsala University in 1843.
Indologist and historian Otto Grohma completed his Ph.D. at the University of Vienna (~1963–1971) and became an assistant there in 1972.

Otto Heinrich Wilhelm Keller worked in linguistics and Iranian studies, completing his Ph.D. at Giessen under Christian Bartholomae (1897–1904). He served as Oberlehrer at Oppenheim (1908), director at Michelstadt (1918), and Oberstudiendirektor at Wolfgang-Ernst-Gymnasium (1925–1935).

Linguist Otto Hoffmann earned his Ph.D. at Göttingen under August Fick (1883–1888). He taught as privatdozent and associate professor at Königsberg, followed by ordinary professorships in Indo-European linguistics at Breslau (1907–1909) and Münster (1909–1935).

Religious studies scholar Otto Huth completed his Ph.D. at the University of Bonn (1925–1932) after studying theology at Kiel and Marburg. He served as privatdozent at Strasbourg (1941–1944) and as privatdozent (1939) and professor (1942–1971) at the University of Tübingen.

Otto Höfler was a scholar of linguistics and religious studies who earned his Ph.D. (1920–1926) and habilitation (~1928–1931) at the University of Vienna, studying under Rudolf Much. He held professorships at Kiel (1935), Munich (1938–1945, 1954), and Vienna (1957–1971).

Otto Jahn was an archaeologist and linguist who studied at Kiel, Leipzig, and Berlin. He held academic posts at Kiel University (~1839–1842), University of Greifswald (~1842–1847), University of Leipzig (~1847–1851), and University of Bonn (~1855–1869).

Religious and Buddhist studies scholar Otto K. Schwarz earned a Master of Economics from the Financial University (2006–2011) and a PhD from the Russian Christian Academy for the Humanities (2021–2025). He joined the Higher School of Economics faculty in 2026.
